summary: Notes from a meeting about the status of DNSSEC, the DNS security extensions. It records where the technology stood at the time. It is a memo, not a specification.

eli5.summary: These are a team's meeting notes about how far along their project to protect the phone book was.

questions: why is dnssec hard to deploy
subtitle: Status update on security extensions for the DNS system.

tldr.problem: The Domain Name System needs protection against tampering and spoofing, but the security extensions (DNSSEC) were still under development and not widely deployed.
tldr.mechanism: DNSSEC is a toolbox of techniques including digital signatures (RFC 2535), TSIG for transaction authentication, secure dynamic updates, and CERT records for distribution of security data.
tldr.outcome: Multiple organizations were working on implementation and deployment, but DNSSEC remained immature and challenging to deploy at the time this document was written in 2001.

facts.label: Organizations attending
facts.value: 12+ including NLnet Labs, Verisign, CAIRN, NIST, DISA, RIPE NCC

today: RFC 2535 was later obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, which provided updated specifications incorporating experience from deployments. DNSSEC is now an Internet Standard (STD 63), though widespread adoption has been gradual.

sections.title: The DNSSEC Toolbox
sections.content:
RFC 3130 summarizes a 2001 meeting about the Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC), a collection of techniques to protect DNS from tampering and spoofing attacks. DNSSEC is not a single protocol but a toolbox of four main components. Digital signature protection (RFC 2535) allows DNS zones to be signed and verified at scale. TSIG (RFC 2845) provides transaction-level authentication for queries and zone transfers using shared secrets. Secure dynamic updates (RFC 3007) let DNS records be safely modified. Finally, the CERT resource record (RFC 2538) allows DNS to carry certificates, making it a distribution mechanism for security data.

The current state was summarized as important, a buzzword, hard, and immature. No single implementation fully covered all parts, and deployment was extremely limited.
sections.eli5: DNSSEC is like a toolbox with locks, signature cards, ways to safely update the phone book, and certificates. Groups were building these tools, but they were still under construction and complicated to use.

sections.title: Organization Efforts and Goals
sections.content: Multiple organizations were actively working on DNSSEC. NLnet Labs studied the impact on country code domains, tested signing large zones, and proposed simplified key rollover procedures. Verisign examined what it would take to offer DNSSEC as a service for large zones like .com. The Foundation for Internet Infrastructure in Sweden studied the administrative complexity of coordinating between registries, registrars, registrants, and DNS operators—four parties that might or might not be separate organizations. RSSAC (Root Server System Advisory Committee) endorsed deploying TSIG but wanted to understand the impact of other DNSSEC components before introducing them into production root servers. CAIRN (a DARPA-funded research network) worked on building chains of trust when parts of the DNS tree were unavailable. NIST was collecting performance data to quantify DNSSEC's impact on DNS server workload. DISA funded DNSSEC implementation in BIND. RIPE NCC and ARIN were exploring DNSSEC for reverse DNS zones.
sections.eli5: Lots of different groups were testing DNSSEC on different parts of the network: phone book registries, Internet researchers, and companies that run big DNS systems. Each group was trying to solve different pieces of the puzzle.

sections.title: Key Open Questions
sections.content: The meeting identified four critical questions facing DNSSEC deployment. First, is it deployable, and when? The usual answer was "not now, maybe in about a year," but workshops held since 1999 were making progress. The meeting concluded that longer-term test deployments—not just one or two-day workshops—were needed to assess issues involving the passage of time, such as key expiration and revalidation. Second, does DNSSEC work? Most effort went into making the existing specification work, though some research continued on whether the proposed NXT record (for proving that a name does not exist) was the right approach. There was little doubt about the value of KEY and SIG records, but research was still needed on validating keys across zone boundaries. Third, how will client software use DNSSEC? Some groups were integrating it into applications like secure shell, but it was unclear whether operating systems would support DNSSEC in their standard name resolution routines. Fourth, what are the remaining issues? The main ones were the NXT record design, and parent validation of child zone signatures—particularly the operational procedures, not just the protocol.
sections.eli5: The big questions were: Can we actually use this? Does it work the right way? How will programs talk to it? What else needs to be fixed? These are the kinds of questions you ask when a project is still being figured out.

sections.title: Path to Draft Standard
sections.content: For DNSSEC to progress from Proposed Standard to Draft Standard under RFC 2026, two requirements had to be met: there must be two or more interoperable implementations, and there must be sufficient successful operational experience. In 2001, only BIND was being seriously fitted with DNSSEC support (v8.2 had partial support, v9 was the first full implementation). To demonstrate interoperability, a second independent DNSSEC implementation was needed within 18 months. The DNSEXT working group was beginning a rewrite of RFC 2535 to incorporate implementation and testing experience, while DNSOP was the forum for operations documents. The working group also needed contributions from the community on operational topics.
sections.eli5: To make DNSSEC an official standard, two different groups of programmers had to build it independently and show it actually works in real networks. At the time, only one group was doing this seriously.
